newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup - Howard steers alone.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup - Howard steers alone.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
When the Prime Minister decides to change tack, he sometimes neglects to give the crew fair warning.
There are indications this week that his first mate, Peter Costello, is getting a bit tetchy about being forced to duck the swinging boom as the good ship government abruptly changes course.
Last night's "pragmatic" car tariff decision to freeze protection at 15 percent until 2005 is but the latest decision to build tension between the Treasurer and his leader.
Costello had backed the Productivity Commission's recommendations for a five percent tariff by 2005; his department regards the outcome as a bad decision.
But on broad policy Costello isn't alone. That giant backbench is also showing signs of mutiny unless it's consulted more regularly and broadly.
Among the backbench members' whinges are changes to health, education and Richard Alston's new grand plan to ease the cross media laws and relax the sector's foreign ownership restrictions.
But casting a bigger shadow in the future is tax. Once again the backbench, and most of the ministry, were caught short by the slam dunk nature of John Howard's shift on the subject.

One Queensland member, faced with questions from his constituents, rose in the weekly meetings of the Liberal and National parties one day late last year to inquire whether the government would be leading the community into a tax reform debate.

Howard aggressively put him down, embarrassing him in front of his colleagues. It was a more strident version of the sort of thing Howard was saying publicly as recently as January: "One of the dangers of the current rhetoric about tax reform in Australia is that we run the risk of seeing it as a great economic elixir."
The backbencher trudged off back to his electorate to tell his constituents the news -- no tax reform and, in particular, no GST.

Just a few months later the hapless member was watching weekend television to see the prime minister suddenly advocating tax reform: "There's no doubt that at some stage, sooner or later, we will have to reform the Australian taxation system." Question: "Does that include revisiting a GST?" Answer: "Well, you can't have a reform unless you look at all of the options."

Imagine his surprise. And his consternation in the weeks since as the prime minister's rhetoric has been wound up to the point where this week he declared that opponents of tax reform and a GST (read Kim Beazley) were "yesterday's men chasing yesterday's taxation system".
What has prompted this bewildering shift? According to the Howard camp, the catalyst was the New South Wales bed tax.
They'll explain that Bob Carr's new incursion into indirect taxes threw open the door to all the states expanding their indirect tax base, leaving the Commonwealth trailing.

But that's not the whole story. For some time Howard advisers have been concerned that the electoral cycle was slipping by and the government still had no viable strategy for dealing with the inevitable question: Would it introduce a GST in its second term?

The worst outcome for the coalition would be to find itself hard up against the next election still with no rational answer. And, of course, the lack of a plan would severely restrict its options on the timing of any election. Whatever the basis of an election, tax would be sure to rear its head before too long.

And there was another spur. Deepening the complication posed by the states is the looming High Court judgement on state franchise fees -- the tobacco "tax" alone raises between A$6.0 billion and A$7.0 billion a year for the states.
They want to know if the so-called fees are legal and whether they can be extended into other areas, in effect raising the prospect of a states' GST.
That will be handed down by the full bench of the court in August and will bring the whole question of indirect taxes to a head, one way or the other.
Meanwhile, "yesterday's men" on the opposition benches this week have made heavy weather of scoring against a government which is offering plenty of openings, including tax.
Labor's Achilles heel this year was always going to be its policy rewrite process in the lead-up to its national conference next January.

A leaked copy of front bencher Lindsay Tanner's policy paper revealed not all is well in the party. Tanner had a shot at those (led by industry spokesman Simon Crean) who wish to return to a prescriptive industry policy, including tariff freezes.

"It is essential we do not lapse into vacuous populism and merely recycle old ideas. Building a society based on economic security, a fair balance between economic efficiency and social equity and a broad capacity to participate requires new ideas and initiatives, not a trip down memory lane arm-in-arm with Pauline Hanson," Tanner's paper said.
That would have been a one-day wonder. But Kim Beazley managed to turn it into a good old-fashioned internal Labor stoush by reading the riot act to his shadow ministry, using words like "treason".
That didn't take long to become public either. It's ensured the rest of the policy review will be tense to say the least.
All in all, trouble at mill.
-- Reuter Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
